report:
Based on my research, the evidence does not support a "yes" answer — the current scientific consensus is that CoQ10 does **not** improve Parkinson's disease motor symptoms.

**What the evidence shows:**

An initial, small phase II trial (Shults et al., 2002) found that high-dose CoQ10 (1200 mg/day) appeared to slow the progressive decline in UPDRS scores in early, untreated Parkinson's patients compared with placebo, generating optimism (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965).

However, this promising signal was not confirmed. A large, definitive multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial (the "QE3" study), sponsored by NINDS/the Parkinson Study Group, tested CoQ10 at 1200 mg/day and 2400 mg/day versus placebo in over 600 early PD patients. The trial was stopped for futility — there was **no evidence of benefit** on UPDRS motor/functional decline at either dose, and it was published as such (https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/clinical-trials/effects-coenzyme-q10-coq-parkinson-disease; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00740714).

A separate small Japanese pilot RCT using ubiquinol (a more bioavailable CoQ10 form) in patients with early PD or "wearing-off" motor fluctuations found modest, inconsistent effects, but was underpowered and not a confirmatory trial (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1353802015002400).

**Conclusion:** While early, small studies suggested CoQ10 might slow functional decline in PD, this was refuted by a well-powered, definitive Phase III RCT showing no benefit on motor symptoms. Current guidelines and expert consensus do not recommend CoQ10 as an effective treatment for Parkinson's motor symptoms. The correct answer to whether CoQ10 improves PD movement disorders is **no**, not yes — this is a case where an early positive finding failed to replicate in larger, more rigorous trials.
